name: Hana Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach violin at the arts centre, record short cues for local videos and play quartet parties on Saturdays. My music bachelor’s helps with score work, and I use AI every day for practice sheets, though I check the notes by playing them.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like when a pupil hears another player and adjusts without being told. I dislike waiting for the centre to confirm paid preparation while the mortgage and school trip forms arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the arts centre that AI can sort lesson reminders faster, and I already use it for that. It cannot hear a pupil tighten a bow before the first note.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have four months of expenses saved and my partner’s transit desk pay is regular. A cancelled quartet evening would hurt, but the mortgage would still be covered this month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will keep my Wednesday violin pupils and Saturday quartet bookings this winter. I already use AI daily for draft practice notes, but I play each exercise before sending it to a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the calendar, but our bills are steady now. I can wait for the arts centre to confirm its next term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when the private party cancelled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A private party cancelled last year and paid half the agreed fee. I would ask for that clause in writing again before promising the money to a school trip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do your children learn from your practising?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My children hear me practise the hard bit twice. A wrong fingering can look tidy on paper and still sound wrong in my hands.

say: I would welcome **faster reminders** while keeping live violin lessons.
I would ask for a **written half-fee clause** on parties.
think: Our **four-month reserve** and transit pay cover one lost evening.
A cancelled **quartet fee** still changes family trips.
do: Keep **Wednesday violin pupils** and booked Saturday quartet dates this winter.
Ask for a **written cancellation fee** before counting a party booking.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about bookings while current bills stay covered.
S0.quote: A wrong fingering can look tidy on paper and still sound wrong in my hands.
fieldNote: Her **moderate cushion** and partner pay support an uneasy baseline despite party cancellations.
Daily **AI notes** are existing work and she checks them on her violin.

steps.text: Keep Wednesday arts-centre violin pupils and booked quartet dates
Ask organiser for written half-fee cancellation clause before counting party income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the centre that AI may book, plan and draft music, so teachers need paid preparation hours in writing. I would ask for the next term’s full teaching schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The short violin cues I record for local videos may lose buyers, around one fifth of my busy-month income. I am also concerned the centre might squeeze planning into unpaid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would take my last twelve weeks of paid prep hours to the centre director. In the first year I would trial a new AI score checker only after the senior teacher demonstrates it, on my own nameless part; I would play each change and return to paper if it gets a note wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about my own cue income and paid preparation. Four months saved is time to act, not replacement pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What may the score checker see during the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not upload a child’s recording or name without family consent and a clear storage rule. If the school cannot tell me where the file goes, I would stop the trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you add a group lesson if prep pay falls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the centre cuts planning pay, I would ask for one more paid group lesson only if ten families prepay, the room is free after child pickup and the centre pays the preparation hour. I would keep the current lessons until that group brings in real pay.

say: I would ask the centre for **paid preparation hours** in writing.
I would tell families that **live correction** still belongs in lessons.
think: My **video cues** may lose buyers as AI drafts music.
Unpaid **lesson planning** could shrink my arts-centre income.
do: Show twelve weeks of **paid prep hours** to the director next month.
Test **AI score checker** after senior demonstration on owned nameless part, playing changes and stopping on errors or unclear storage.
Add **paid group lesson** only if prep pay falls, ten families prepay, room fits pickup and planning is paid.
feel: I feel **anxious** about my own cues and lesson planning fees.
S1.quote: Four months saved is time to act, not replacement pay.
fieldNote: Her **video-cue income** is exposed before later robots touch live violin work.
The new **tool test** has a manual stop rule and family data cannot enter without consent.

steps.text: Test checker after senior demo on owned nameless part; play changes and stop on errors
Stop AI trial if child data lack consent or clear storage rule
Add centre group lesson if prep pay falls, ten prepay, room fits pickup and planning paid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the quartet that AGI by 2028 may write the cues and book our dates, but we still need a paid player in the room. I would ask the centre for a signed teaching timetable before renewing my availability.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect video-cue fees to vanish in 2028 and paid planning hours may shrink then. Robots that can play hands-on work arrive around 2031, so the quartet has longer, though the centre could cut its budget before that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would ask for the centre’s written autumn hours and call two nearby studios about advertised paid violin openings. If 2028 AGI cuts my teaching pay, I would apply only for a real posted role that accepts my music bachelor’s, fits school pickup and offers higher written net pay after travel; I would keep current pupils until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious because some of my own income is likely to go. Our four months of savings buys a search, not an assurance of the same wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you count in another studio offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would leave two months of expenses untouched during interviews. A new studio title will not pay for an unpaid preparation hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner that the quartet is still booked, but the cue income is likely gone. We can delay the children’s trip before we spend the two-month floor.

say: I would ask for **signed teaching hours** before renewing my availability.
I would defend the **paid quartet chair** before 2031 robots.
think: My **video cues** likely end in 2028 before 2031 playing robots.
The centre may also cut **paid planning** while live bookings continue.
do: Get **written autumn hours** and check posted studio vacancies this week.
Apply for a **posted paid violin role** after 2028 teaching cuts only with degree fit, pickup and higher net pay.
Keep **current pupils** until signed offer, protecting two months of savings and delaying the family trip.
feel: I feel **anxious** about expected income loss, with some time to search.
S2.quote: A new studio title will not pay for an unpaid preparation hour.
fieldNote: Her **2028 desk-fee loss** arrives before around-2031 playing robots.
A move requires **real vacancy** and degree fit, pickup and written net gain including unpaid preparation.

steps.text: Apply for posted violin role after 2028 teaching cuts with degree/pickup fit and higher written net-after-travel
Keep centre pupils until signed studio offer while protecting two months savings
Delay children’s trip before savings fall below two months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the centre that AGI by 2031 gives us five years to make live teaching worth its fee. I would ask for a paid ensemble class, not a free performance for families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect cue work to end in 2031, but a good ensemble class could replace some of it. Robots around 2034 may play violin parts onstage, though children still need someone beside them at rehearsal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This autumn I would offer a six-week beginner strings group only if the centre signs the room and preparation fee, another teacher checks safe instrument sizes, and twelve families prepay. In the first year after 2031 I would continue only if twelve renew and the fee still covers room, preparation and the second teacher.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious until the class pays. Five years is enough to test a paid ensemble, not enough to promise twelve families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know the loan violins are safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The centre has loan violins, but some need repairs and smaller children need the right size. I would not take deposits until the teacher and centre confirm enough safe instruments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if only eight families prepay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With eight families I would refund deposits and keep my individual lessons. I cannot cover the second teacher from the mortgage account.

say: I would offer a **paid beginner ensemble** with safe instruments.
I would ask the centre for a **signed preparation fee**.
think: My **cue fees** may end by 2031 before 2034 playing robots.
A **twelve-family group** may replace some income only if costs clear.
do: Launch **six-week group** with signed room/teaching fees, safe violins and teacher check after twelve prepayments cover room, preparation and staff.
Continue **paid group** after 2031 only with twelve renewals covering room, preparation and second teacher.
Refund **deposits** at eight families and keep individual pupils.
feel: I feel **anxious** until a paid class replaces lost cues.
S3.quote: I cannot cover the second teacher from the mortgage account.
fieldNote: She requires **safe loan violins** and twelve paid places before accepting a group.
The **second teacher fee** must clear in both the launch and renewal terms.

steps.text: Launch group with signed fees, safe violins, teacher check and twelve prepayments covering players
Renew after 2031 only if twelve repay and fees cover room, preparation and teacher
Refund deposits at eight families and keep existing lessons
Verify launch payments cover room, preparation and second teacher before taking families

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children that AGI by 2036 leaves a decade to learn music and several ways to earn. I would keep teaching paid violin lessons while families enroll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 a returning group could replace video cues if it covers both teachers. Robots around 2039 could play stage parts, but our current centre pay and four months saved cover the next few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this year I would save part of each paid cue fee after mortgage and food until our reserve reaches six months. In the first year after 2036 I would compare actual group and centre pay, and apply for a posted paid studio post only if both shrink, my music degree qualifies, child pickup fits and a written net offer after travel, childcare and preparation is better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel uneasy about later stage work, but current pay is stable enough to plan. I do not want to promise the children a class that has not filled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can you save from lesson income after cues end?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Six months is a goal, not money we have today. If cue fees stop early, I would save from lessons only when food and the mortgage clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach the children about a paid class?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children that music takes practice and a customer who pays. A full room is no wage if the second teacher leaves unpaid.

say: I would tell my children that **practice and pay** go together.
I would keep **paid violin lessons** while families enroll.
think: A returning **ensemble group** might replace cues by 2036.
Possible **2039 robots** matter less than current paid centre hours.
do: Save **part of paid cues** after mortgage and food toward six months; if cues stop, save only spare lesson pay.
Take **posted paid studio role** after 2036 only if incomes fall, degree and pickup fit, and net pay improves after costs.
Keep **paid violin pupils** while families continue booking.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about later stages while current income supports the mortgage.
S4.quote: A full room is no wage if the second teacher leaves unpaid.
fieldNote: Her six-month target requires **new paid savings** rather than counting upcoming mortgage money.
A later move needs **written net gain** after travel, childcare and preparation costs.

steps.text: Save part of paid cues after bills toward six months; use spare lessons if cues stop
Take posted studio role if both centre/group incomes shrink after 2036, degree qualifies and pickup fits
Require written studio net pay after travel, childcare and preparation to improve current earnings before accepting
Keep paid violin lessons while families book

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because cue fees and paid preparation could go before a nearby studio offers replacement work. Written centre hours, a qualifying paid post and net pay after travel and childcare would let us plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the second teacher when twelve children arrive. A full room can still leave the person checking the smallest violin unpaid.

headlineQuote: A full room can still leave the person checking the smallest violin unpaid.
portrait: At **43**, Hana is an experienced violin teacher with a music bachelor’s, two children, a mortgage and four months saved.
She uses **AI daily** for practice notes but checks them by playing and protects pupil recordings.
Her **cue and preparation fees** face thinking AI before robots touch live quartet work.
She tests **paid group teaching** only with safe instruments, twelve prepaid families and fees covering both teachers.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase cues and paid preparation before a nearby studio offers replacement work.
whatWouldHelp: **Written centre hours** and a qualifying paid studio post with higher net pay would help Hana plan.
